newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian government delighted with poultry ruling.
newsitem.headline: Canadian government delighted with poultry ruling.

text.p: The Canadian government on Monday welcomed the unanimous decision by a NAFTA panel that Canada's tariffs on dairy, poultry and egg imports were allowed under the North American Free Trade Agreement.
"The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) panel has determined that Canadian tariffs conform fully with the provisions of the North American Free Trade Agreement," a government statement said.
"The government is very pleased with this decisive and unanimous ruling made by the five panel members," International Trade Minister Art Eggleton stated.
"This case underlines the value of the NAFTA panel process where disputes can be settled on their merits," Eggleton added.
"The panel is great news for Canada and the country's entire agriculture industry," Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale declared in a statement.

The statement said the United States had challenged Canada's right under the NAFTA to apply tariffs that were agreed to in the World Trade Organizaton (WTO) agreement on imports of U.S. dairy, poultry, egg, margarine and barley products.
Canada had converted its former quotas on products like dairy, poultry and eggs into large tariffs, and maintained that this was consistent with its obligations under both the WTO and NAFTA.

"In its ruling, the panel agreed that provisions in the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement allowed Canada to maintain quantitative import restrictions against certain U.S. imports," the statement said. "It also concluded that Canada was obliged to end its quantitative import restrictions under the WTO Agreement and that Canada had the right to convert them into tariff equivalents under the WTO and the NAFTA."
Under the WTO deal, which took effect at the start of 1995, Canada applied tariffs of 25 to 350 percent on the agricultural imports on which it agreed to convert its quotas.
WTO members were required to provide access at lower tariff rates for imports up to specified levels.
But the ruling assured that the Canada's supply management would not now be swamped by imports of cheaper American milk, eggs or chicken.

The statement pointed out, nonetheless, that the United States has managed to increase its exports in poultry and egg products to Canada by 120 percent to C$298.5 million in 1995 compared with 1988, while dairy products rose 141 percent over the period to C$56 million.
That was dwarfed by the C$6.4 billion that the statement said Canada's supply-managed commodity sector is worth -- covering dairy products, chicken, turkey eggs and broiler hatching eggs.
